oil.summary: WTI surged through the psychologically critical $100/bbl level, settling at $101.67 (+5.86%), while Brent followed at $106.98 (+5.70%), extending a month-long rally of roughly 20-22%. The primary catalyst is an escalating U.S.-Iran tanker conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, with the U.S. striking Iranian oil tankers and Iran responding with threats of economic warfare and missile action while the Houthis simultaneously attacked Saudi Arabia. Tanker rates hit record highs as operators reprice Middle East routing risk. A draw of 400,000 barrels in U.S. crude inventories for the week ending September 4 provided an additional supportive signal. HSBC raised its full-year 2026 Brent forecast to $90, still well below spot, suggesting further analyst upgrades may follow. RBOB gasoline was the odd one out, slipping 1.07% on the day despite the crude surge.
drivers: U.S.-Iran tanker strikes escalating in Strait of Hormuz, sharply tightening seaborne crude supply routes
U.S. crude inventory draw of 400,000 barrels for the week ending September 4 reinforces tight physical market
Record tanker freight rates and Iran's threat of further economic warfare sustaining geopolitical risk premium

gas.summary: TTF rallied 3.43% on the day to €81.965/MWh, building on a punishing 39.55% one-month run as two distinct supply-side shocks compounded each other. Ukrainian drones struck two Russian gas facilities approximately 3,200 km inside Russian territory in a record-setting deep strike on Arctic gas infrastructure, raising fresh questions about Russian export capacity. Simultaneously, the Strait of Hormuz crisis continues to choke LNG flows, with the IEA flagging that soaring LNG prices are forcing economies toward coal as a substitute, pushing global coal demand toward record highs. Australia softened its domestic gas reservation rules for LNG exporters, a marginal supply-side concession. Permian basin gas remains structurally oversupplied locally—negative-value days totaling 118 this year—underscoring the stark bifurcation between U.S. basin prices and elevated international benchmarks.
drivers: Ukrainian drone strike on two Russian Arctic gas facilities at record 3,200 km range threatens Russian export supply
Hormuz LNG disruption driving global gas prices sharply higher, pushing coal substitution per IEA
Australia easing domestic gas reservation rules for LNG exporters, offering modest relief on the margin

power.summary: EU carbon EUAs edged up a modest 0.48% to $81.555/EUA, with the one-month gain of 4.68% appearing restrained relative to the explosive moves in the underlying fuel complex. The dominant cross-market pressure point is TTF at €81.965/MWh (+39.55% over the month), which is structurally bearish for gas-fired power economics and is accelerating coal-to-gas switching in reverse, per the IEA. The methane emissions headline flags a widening global divide in abatement progress, a longer-term carbon market structural factor. Chevron's planned Permian power plant signals that stranded basin gas may find an outlet in behind-the-meter generation rather than pipeline flows. Overall, the carbon complex is notably calm relative to the fuel shock; thin headline flow here limits deeper analysis.
drivers: TTF at €81.965/MWh (+39.55% one month) compressing gas-fired power margins and incentivising coal burn, mildly supportive for EUAs
IEA warning of record coal demand as LNG supply tightens could lift medium-term carbon compliance demand
Widening global divide in methane abatement progress adding uncertainty to long-run carbon market trajectory
